name: Interaction Results: full prose before figure
old:
Context and ancestry determine which branches should receive a signal. Interactions between branches can also change the signal's sign and magnitude from example to example. We tested this distinction on tasks with identical input-sensitivity spectra, after ensuring that the same tree could represent both targets. This separates a limitation of credit delivery from a limitation of the forward computation.

Eight independent inputs $x_i$ took values $-1$ or $+1$ with equal probability. Each branch combined its left and right child outputs as $u=a+bu_L+cu_R+du_Lu_R$, with four trainable coefficients. Such a unit is multi-affine: it is affine in either child while the other is fixed. Pairwise targets summed four disjoint products, $f_M=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in M}s_{ij}x_ix_j$; quartic targets summed products over two complementary quartets, $f_A=\frac12(s_A\prod_{i\in A}x_i+s_{\bar A}\prod_{i\notin A}x_i)$. Here $M$ partitions the inputs into pairs, $A$ is one quartet and $\bar A$ its complement. Signs $s$ were independently sampled. Within each seed, both targets shared a compatible balanced tree, input assignment, initial weights and example streams (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}A). Both have input-sensitivity second moment $\E[\nabla_xf\nabla_xf^{\mathsf T}]=I_8/4$: the strengths of independent input-sensitivity directions are identical.

Compatibility has an exact criterion in this model. At each subtree boundary, arrange the target's interaction coefficients in a matrix indexed by products of inputs inside and outside that subtree. After removing the constant inside row, this matrix must have rank at most one, because only one scalar leaves the branch. This condition is also sufficient when it holds at every boundary; discarded singular values bound representation error (Methods; Supplementary Section~S4). It is a prerequisite for the credit comparison, not a theorem about the learning rule. Boolean examples and the complete structure census are retained in Supplementary Figs.~S36--S37 and S43--S44.

We compared exact path credit with unit broadcast and an initially calibrated spatial profile. The calibrated rule averaged each student's path derivatives over 256 unlabeled initialization examples and kept that six-site profile fixed during learning. It could therefore preserve initial signs and relative gains without access to the target. All rules used exact local eligibilities and the same scalar output error. Three development seeds selected learning rates with equal tuning budgets; twenty fresh paired seeds then tested the frozen choices. A separate nested target summed products over prefixes of two, four, six and eight inputs on its own compatible tree.

After 1,024 Adam steps, exact and calibrated credit achieved mean held-out normalized mean squared error (NMSE) of 0.0317 and 0.0236 on pairwise targets, compared with 0.1516 and 0.9813 on quartic targets (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}B,C). NMSE divides squared prediction error by the clean target variance. On nested targets, exact and calibrated NMSE were 0.0230 and 0.7690 (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}D). The predefined task-by-credit contrast was the calibrated-minus-exact gap for quartic targets minus the same gap for pairwise targets: 0.838 NMSE (95\% paired seed-bootstrap interval, 0.719--0.931), positive in all twenty seeds. A common learning rate gave 0.843 (0.727--0.935; Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}E). These are fixed-budget comparisons; some exact quartic fits retained appreciable error. Equal additive label noise produced different NMSE floors because pairwise and quartic targets have variances one and one-half, respectively.

The learned credit fields explain a distinction that the input spectrum misses. Let $\bm q(x)$ contain the six nonsomatic derivatives of root output with respect to branch output. Exact branch credit is scalar output error times $\bm q$. We first measured how much of the path field's ensemble energy the best single fixed spatial profile could reproduce, allowing an oracle amplitude for each example. At exact-trained checkpoints, that profile captured 99.7\% of pairwise path-field energy, but only 46.1\% for quartic and 44.8\% for nested targets (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}F). The separation persisted after loss-error and eligibility weighting and in site-normalized spectra; a replay of 600 earlier fits replicated it (Supplementary Section~S4). Uniform-profile capture did not separate the families: a nearly one-dimensional field can have a signed, nonuniform direction. Fixed positive profile scaling largely cancels in Adam, explaining the nearly identical calibrated and sign-only trajectories. Exact path factors vary across examples and training, so this identity alone does not explain their slower pairwise learning.

Thus identical input spectra can accompany different learned credit spectra on the same tree, and fixed-profile learning fails where the trained field varies in more spatial directions. At identical weights and inputs, however, path derivatives are target-independent. The spectrum is a property of the learner's state and coordinates, not a task-only initialization diagnostic. These observations support a role for example-dependent spatial credit without establishing that all six independent channels, or exact gradients, are necessary.

The effect has a useful boundary. On a compatible positive-conductance teacher, every tested fixed-profile rule learned accurately with Adam; exact credit added no practical accuracy benefit. Boolean controls likewise distinguished cases: broadcast learned aligned XOR-of-AND, whereas parity showed a large exact-credit advantage under the tested optimizer (Supplementary Figs.~S42--S44). Interaction structure therefore identifies comparisons worth testing, rather than a universal monotonic law of credit resolution. Estimating interactions from noisy examples also yielded useful trees; the estimator and its learning pipeline remain supporting structure-design results in Supplementary Figs.~S41--S42.
new:
Interactions across branches can change credit's sign and magnitude between examples. We compared targets with identical input-sensitivity spectra on the same representationally compatible tree, separating credit delivery from forward capacity.

Eight independent inputs $x_i$ were equally likely to be $-1$ or $+1$. Each branch computed $u=a+bu_L+cu_R+du_Lu_R$ with four trainable coefficients. This multi-affine unit is affine in either child while the other is fixed. Pairwise targets summed four disjoint products, $f_M=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in M}s_{ij}x_ix_j$; quartic targets combined complementary quartets, $f_A=\frac12(s_A\prod_{i\in A}x_i+s_{\bar A}\prod_{i\notin A}x_i)$. Here $M$ partitions inputs into pairs, $A$ is one quartet, $\bar A$ its complement, and signs $s$ were independently sampled. Within each seed, targets shared a compatible balanced tree, input assignment, initial weights and examples (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}A). Both have input-sensitivity second moment $\E[\nabla_xf\nabla_xf^{\mathsf T}]=I_8/4$, giving identical strengths of independent sensitivity directions.

Compatibility has an exact criterion. At each subtree boundary, arrange interaction coefficients into a matrix indexed by products of inputs inside and outside the subtree. Removing the constant inside row must leave rank at most one, because only one scalar leaves the branch. This condition is necessary and sufficient across all boundaries; discarded singular values bound representation error (Methods; Supplementary Section~S4). It constrains forward capacity, not the learning rule. Boolean examples and the structure census appear in Supplementary Figs.~S36--S37 and S43--S44.

All credit rules used the same exact local eligibilities and scalar output error. We compared exact paths with unit broadcast and a fixed six-site profile calibrated from each student's mean path derivatives over 256 unlabeled initialization examples. Three development seeds selected learning rates with equal budgets; twenty fresh paired seeds tested the frozen choices. A separate nested target summed products over prefixes of two, four, six and eight inputs on its own compatible tree.

After 1,024 Adam steps, exact/calibrated held-out normalized mean squared errors (NMSE) were 0.0317/0.0236 for pairwise targets, 0.1516/0.9813 for quartic targets and 0.0230/0.7690 for nested targets (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}B--D). NMSE divides squared prediction error by clean target variance. The predefined quartic-minus-pairwise difference in calibrated-minus-exact gaps was 0.838 (95\% paired seed-bootstrap interval, 0.719--0.931), positive in all twenty seeds; a common rate gave 0.843 (0.727--0.935; Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}E). Some exact quartic fits retained appreciable error at this fixed budget. Equal label noise gave different NMSE floors because pairwise and quartic target variances were one and one-half.

The trained fields reveal a distinction missed by the input spectrum. Let $\bm q(x)$ contain the six nonsomatic derivatives of root output with respect to branch output; exact branch credit is scalar output error times $\bm q$. Allowing an oracle amplitude per example, the best fixed profile captured 99.7\% of exact-trained path-field energy for pairwise targets, but 46.1\% for quartic and 44.8\% for nested targets (Fig.~\ref{fig:prospective}F). Loss-error weighting, eligibility weighting, site-normalized spectra and replay of 600 earlier fits preserved this separation (Supplementary Section~S4). Uniform-profile capture did not: a nearly one-dimensional field can have a signed, nonuniform direction. Positive fixed-profile scaling largely cancels in Adam, explaining calibrated/sign-only agreement; it does not explain the slower pairwise learning with changing exact paths.

Thus input-matched targets developed different credit spectra and tolerance of fixed profiles. At fixed weights and inputs, however, path derivatives are target-independent: their spectrum describes learned states and coordinates, not a task-only initialization diagnostic. Failure of the tested profiles supports example-dependent spatial credit without establishing that six independent channels or exact gradients are necessary.

Additional controls delimit the result. Fixed-profile Adam learned a compatible positive-conductance teacher accurately; broadcast learned aligned XOR-of-AND, whereas parity favored exact credit under the tested optimizer (Supplementary Figs.~S42--S44). Noisy-query interaction estimation also yielded useful trees, retained as supporting structure-design evidence in Supplementary Figs.~S41--S42. Interaction structure therefore motivates specific credit comparisons rather than a universal monotonic resolution law.

name: Discussion: full prose
old:
Task structure changes which spatial distinctions a useful dendritic learning signal must preserve. The route-dictionary framework makes this question explicit: morphology supplies patterns of delivery, a teaching mechanism supplies their coefficients, and conductance controls their gains. The experiments form a progression from neuronal identity to branch selection, ancestry grouping and example-dependent credit across interacting branches. Useful resolution depends on the task and learner, beyond anatomical detail or exact-gradient fidelity alone.

Image tasks locate a substantial first step at the neuron boundary. Supplying distinct neuronal coordinates accounts for most of the performance gain, including when a random map provides between-neuron feedback. Contextual conflict then creates a need to distinguish active from inactive branches, a distinction that can be supplied either in feedback or by gating local eligibility. Hierarchical distractors create a smaller advantage for ancestry at limited bandwidth. Its four-route location follows from the generator's coefficients, making the experiment a test of a designed prediction about grouping rather than evidence for a universal optimum. These comparisons separate the information delivered from the physical substrate that carries it.

The interaction comparison links task structure to the learned spatial credit field. Pairwise and quartic targets with identical input-sensitivity spectra share an exactly compatible tree, yet produce different learned credit spectra and sharply different tolerance of fixed spatial profiles. Initial gain calibration and a common learning rate do not remove this difference. A nearly one-dimensional pairwise field can still have poor uniform-broadcast capture, so the relevant issue is the available spatial direction as well as its dimension. The measured spectra describe learned states; they cannot retrospectively validate the failed initialization selector. Nor does failure of the tested profiles establish that every compartment needs an independent external error. Intermediate dictionaries, adaptive profiles and alternative dynamics remain candidate solutions.

Forward structure sets the conditions under which a credit comparison is informative. The cut criterion identifies representationally compatible trees in the scalar multi-affine model, connecting input grouping to hierarchical tensor descriptions \citep{hackbusch2009tensor,grasedyck2010hierarchical,cohen2016tensor}. It also permits constructive structure estimation from noisy examples, retained here as supporting evidence. Conductance trees show both possibilities: simple credit learns some compatible teachers accurately, whereas opposing branch tuning under context-dependent inhibition benefits strongly from routed credit. Three supplied patterns suffice in that experiment, connecting the dictionary proposal to learning in a conductance circuit. Serial composition likewise helps with distributed nuisance factors. Longer training preserves its depth benefit but reverses the LocalCA accuracy advantage of exact credit, which still yields lower cross-entropy. These results explain why task rank, physical depth and feedback resolution should not be treated as interchangeable quantities.

Reconstructed arbors extend the dictionary proposal to measured geometry. Giving all controls the same common broadcast reveals ancestry capacity in the residual modeled field, including the disjoint 47-cell cohort. The smaller contrast against degree--depth surrogates identifies the contribution beyond coarse geometry. Focal shunting supplies a complementary link to biophysics: in a passive tree its adjoint effect reweights the shunt site's ancestry partition, while synaptic driving forces contribute additional local changes. The electrotonic boundary specifies when those changes remain spatially selective. This account concerns transport of sensitivity and differs from inhibition that computes errors or forward gain--load regulation \citep{rossbroich2023disinhibitory,galloni2026cellular,greedy2026celltype,safaai2026gainload}.

The measured-response analyses delimit the biological claim. Ancestry--response similarity provides an empirical structure--function test and shows no preferential alignment in this small cohort. The offline learning comparison principally tests whether a restricted dictionary preserves an almost fixed cable-transfer profile; its sparse selected supports make it a weak test of endogenous route use. A direct biological experiment would compare plasticity below a focal inhibitory site with electrotonically matched off-route sites while matching somatic voltage, first-order current and the outcome signal. Varying conductance state would test the predicted separation between shared and ancestry-selective effects \citep{francioni2026vectorized,cichon2015branch,bloss2016structured}.

The framework complements somatic prediction, segregated teaching, interneuron-mediated errors and burst plasticity \citep{urbanczik2014dendritic,guerguiev2017segregated,sacramento2018dendritic,payeur2021burst}, as well as cable-learning and engineered gating models \citep{bicknell2021synaptic,chavlis2025dendrites,sezener2021gated,iyer2022activedendrites,lv2025dendritic}. Spikes, temporal eligibility, recurrence and full channel kinetics may change both the available profiles and how their coefficients are estimated \citep{bittner2017btsp,magee2020plasticity}. It separates which distinctions the task demands, which routes the arbor offers and which learning can use.
new:
Useful credit resolution depends on the task and learner. Morphology supplies delivery patterns, teaching mechanisms supply their coefficients, and conductance regulates their gains. Image learning benefits mainly from preserving neuronal identity, including with random between-neuron feedback. Contextual conflict requires branch selection, whether supplied by feedback or local eligibility gating. Hierarchical distractors favor ancestry at a bandwidth predicted by the generator's coefficients. These results distinguish useful information from its physical carrier.

The interaction comparison shows why input rank alone is insufficient. Pairwise and quartic targets share input-sensitivity spectra and a compatible tree but develop different credit spectra and tolerance of fixed profiles, despite initial calibration and common-rate controls. Spatial direction matters alongside dimension: even a nearly one-dimensional field can be poorly captured by uniform broadcast. These are learned-state properties, not retrospective support for the failed initialization selector. Intermediate dictionaries, adaptive profiles and alternative dynamics remain plausible solutions.

Conductance trees connect this distinction to a dendritic computation. Simple credit learns some compatible teachers accurately, whereas opposing branch tuning under contextual inhibition benefits strongly from routed credit; three supplied spatial patterns with oracle coefficients suffice in the tested circuit. Forward compatibility remains essential: the scalar multi-affine cut criterion connects input grouping to hierarchical tensor descriptions and supports structure estimation from noisy examples \citep{hackbusch2009tensor,grasedyck2010hierarchical,cohen2016tensor}. Serial composition likewise helps remove distributed nuisance factors, but longer training reverses the LocalCA accuracy advantage of exact credit while preserving its lower cross-entropy. Task rank, physical depth and credit resolution therefore describe different constraints.

Reconstructed arbors provide ancestry capacity beyond a common broadcast, including in the disjoint 47-cell cohort; degree--depth surrogates explain much of that capacity. Focal shunting supplies a biophysical link by reweighting the baseline-weighted ancestry partition, with additional local changes from synaptic driving forces. Cable state determines their spatial selectivity. This concerns sensitivity transport, distinct from inhibition that computes errors or regulates forward gain and load \citep{rossbroich2023disinhibitory,galloni2026cellular,greedy2026celltype,safaai2026gainload}.

Measured ancestry--response similarity showed no preferential alignment in the small recorded cohort. The offline learning comparison chiefly tests preservation of an almost fixed transfer profile and offers limited evidence about endogenous route use. A direct experiment would compare plasticity below a focal inhibitory site with electrotonically matched off-route sites while matching somatic voltage, first-order current and outcome signal. Changing conductance state would test the predicted separation between shared and ancestry-selective effects \citep{francioni2026vectorized,cichon2015branch,bloss2016structured}.

The framework complements somatic prediction, segregated teaching, interneuron-mediated errors and burst plasticity \citep{urbanczik2014dendritic,guerguiev2017segregated,sacramento2018dendritic,payeur2021burst}, alongside cable-learning and engineered gating models \citep{bicknell2021synaptic,chavlis2025dendrites,sezener2021gated,iyer2022activedendrites,lv2025dendritic}. Spikes, temporal eligibility, recurrence and channel kinetics may change the available profiles and coefficient estimation \citep{bittner2017btsp,magee2020plasticity}. The organizing question remains which task-relevant distinctions the arbor and learning mechanism can jointly preserve.

name: Anatomy opening
old: The artificial tasks show what particular credit patterns can accomplish. We next asked whether reconstructed dendritic geometry supplies useful candidate patterns. MICrONS combines electron-microscopy anatomy and connectivity with co-registered visual responses for a subset of cells \citep{microns2025}. Skeletons, soma positions and mapped contact locations and areas were observed; conductances, voltages and gradient fields were modeled. These analyses therefore test the capacity of measured anatomy to support spatial credit, rather than measure a teaching signal.
new: MICrONS links reconstructed anatomy and connectivity to visual responses \citep{microns2025}. We used observed skeletons, soma positions and mapped contact locations and areas to model conductances, voltages and gradient fields, asking whether measured geometry supplies useful delivery patterns. This tests anatomical capacity rather than observed teaching signals.

name: Anatomy common-mode design: two paragraphs
old:
We first examined fields generated independently of the selected dictionary: modeled gradient changes caused by small focal shunts throughout a reciprocal cable. In the original eight-cell analysis, subtree routes lacked a constant component, whereas depth bins could reproduce an all-site broadcast. That difference mattered. A single broadcast captured 31.4\% of total field energy, close to the 32.6\% rank-one ceiling, but most field energy remained outside it. The original comparison therefore mixed the value of a common signal with that of spatial distinctions.

We corrected this resource mismatch by giving every family one budgeted broadcast column and $K-1$ spatial profiles. We measured both total capture and capture of the field remaining after the common component was removed. The protocol was fixed before extending the analysis to 47 disjoint cells from the same mouse and an independently reconstructed second mouse. Each comparison retained actual matrix rank and nonzero coefficient count, because overlapping routes can spend the same nominal budget on different effective resources (Fig.~\ref{fig:topology}).
new: The fields were gradient changes induced by small focal shunts in reciprocal cables, independently of dictionary selection. In the original eight cells, broadcast captured 31.4\% of field energy, near the 32.6\% rank-one ceiling but leaving most energy outside it. Subtree routes lacked a constant component whereas depth bins could broadcast, confounding common and spatial capacity. We therefore gave every family one budgeted broadcast column and $K-1$ spatial profiles, measuring total and residual-field capture and recording actual rank and nonzero count. The protocol was fixed before extension to 47 disjoint cells from the same mouse and a reconstructed second mouse (Fig.~\ref{fig:topology}).

name: Anatomy cohort limitations
old: The original eight cells showed the same ordering after common-mode correction (Fig.~\ref{fig:topology}D). The Pinky second-mouse analysis also favored ancestry, but only eight of ten qualifying cells had enough input-bearing sites and candidate routes for the eight-column comparison. Those cells had just 9--13 input-bearing sites, and ancestry nearly saturated their residual fields. We retain their lower-budget comparisons and exclusions separately rather than pool them with the larger arbors. The earlier route-generated positive controls remain in Supplementary Figs.~S10, S20 and S27; they demonstrate capacity under imposed alignment and are distinct from this independent-field extension.
new: The original eight cells retained the same ordering (Fig.~\ref{fig:topology}D). In the Pinky second mouse, eight of ten qualifying cells supported the eight-column comparison. Their 9--13 input-bearing sites put ancestry near the residual-capture ceiling, so lower-budget comparisons and exclusions remain separate from the larger arbors. Earlier route-generated positive controls test imposed alignment, distinct from these independent fields (Supplementary Figs.~S10, S20 and S27).

name: Anatomy labeling and cost
old: Anatomical labeling and cost measures constrain the interpretation. Direct E/I labels covered 4.71\% of inputs in the disjoint cohort; the 73.0\% direct-versus-proxy agreement was measured among jointly labeled contacts in the original cohort. Nonzero site-by-route coefficients quantify a delivery-cost proxy, not feedback synapses or metabolic expenditure (Fig.~\ref{fig:topology}E). Geometry, labeling and compression sensitivities are reported in Methods and Supplementary Figs.~S12, S25 and S33. The principal result is that ancestry provides spatial capacity beyond a shared broadcast, under matched common-mode access, with its size depending on the arbor and comparison dictionary.
new: Direct E/I labels covered 4.71\% of disjoint-cohort inputs; the original cohort's 73.0\% direct-versus-proxy agreement concerned jointly labeled contacts. Nonzero site-by-route coefficients are a delivery-cost proxy, not feedback synapses or metabolic expenditure (Fig.~\ref{fig:topology}E). Geometry, labeling and compression sensitivities are in Methods and Supplementary Figs.~S12, S25 and S33.

name: Branch-selection opening
old: A learning signal can be harmful if it reaches a branch that received an input but did not contribute to the output. To test branch selection directly, we used one logistic output unit with \(B\in\{2,4,8\}\) parallel branch weight vectors and no internal forward compartments or conductance nonlinearity (Fig.~\ref{fig:branchconflict}A). A context selected the branch that determined the output, while every branch received an image and formed an ungated local eligibility. This separates the information needed to select a branch from any specifically dendritic implementation.
new: To isolate branch-selective information, we used one logistic output with $B\in\{2,4,8\}$ parallel branch weight vectors and no internal forward compartments or conductance nonlinearity (Fig.~\ref{fig:branchconflict}A). Context selected the branch determining the output, while every branch received an image and formed an ungated local eligibility.

name: Branch-selection equivalence after update equation
old: The indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. The factor \(1/B\) matches scale but supplies no branch information. The selector can be delivered in feedback or supplied by a branch-local eligibility gate; the resulting update is identical (Fig.~\ref{fig:branchconflict}B). Consequently, the experiment tests access to branch-selective information, not a requirement for several independently computed external error values.
new: The indicator $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is one when its condition holds, zero otherwise; $1/B$ matches scale without supplying branch information. A feedback selector and a branch-local eligibility gate give the same update (Fig.~\ref{fig:branchconflict}B), testing access to selection rather than a need for independently computed external errors.

name: Branch-selection conclusion
old: The shared rule reached chance at lower conflict doses as branch count increased, consistent with the predicted shift (Fig.~\ref{fig:branchconflict}F). Five two-branch seeds did not cross in the sampled range. Mean-curve, individual-seed and theoretical crossings are different quantities. Checkpoint diagnostics also showed that gradient alignment changed during learning (Methods; Supplementary Fig.~S29D--F). The causal result is that sending an error to branches that received inputs but did not determine the output can harm learning. A dendritic branch is one possible site for this selection. A separate two-stream task tests the corresponding learning and interference effects (Supplementary Fig.~S19).
new: The shared rule reached chance at lower conflict as branch count increased, consistent with the predicted shift (Fig.~\ref{fig:branchconflict}F); five two-branch seeds never crossed in the sampled range. Theoretical, mean-curve and individual-seed crossings are distinct. Gradient alignment also changed during learning (Methods; Supplementary Fig.~S29D--F). Credit reaching inactive branches can therefore harm learning; dendrites offer one possible selection site. A separate two-stream task tests learning and interference effects (Supplementary Fig.~S19).

name: Introduction conductance paragraph
old: The same anatomical address can transmit a learning signal with different gains as conductance changes. Excitatory and inhibitory contacts open nonnegative conductances whose reversal potentials determine current. Inhibition can lower input resistance and attenuate other inputs even when its own current is small \citep{koch1983nonlinear,holt1997shunting,chance2002gain,gidon2012inhibition,lovettbarron2012regulation}. Conductance state also changes how a local voltage change affects somatic output and task error. A change in channel amplitude rescales a delivery profile; a change in cable transport can reshape the profile itself.
new: Conductance changes the gains of anatomical delivery routes. Excitatory and inhibitory contacts open nonnegative conductances whose reversal potentials determine current; inhibition can lower input resistance and attenuate other inputs even when its own current is small \citep{koch1983nonlinear,holt1997shunting,chance2002gain,gidon2012inhibition,lovettbarron2012regulation}. Channel-amplitude changes rescale a profile, whereas altered cable transport can reshape how local voltage affects somatic output and task error.

name: Introduction final progression paragraph
old: We test a task-to-credit progression: preserving neuron identity on image tasks, selecting the relevant branch under contextual conflict, grouping related branches at limited bandwidth, and resolving example-dependent credit for interactions across branches. Morphology supplies candidate spatial patterns, while conductance controls how those patterns are expressed. Forward representability provides a necessary starting point for interpreting learning, and measured responses test the reach of the anatomical proposal. The central question is which distinctions a useful learning signal must preserve, rather than whether finer feedback is always better.
new: We compare tasks requiring neuronal identity, branch selection, ancestry grouping or example-dependent credit across interacting branches. Morphology supplies candidate patterns and conductance regulates their expression. Forward compatibility anchors the learning comparisons; measured responses test the anatomical proposal. The question is which distinctions useful credit must preserve, rather than whether finer feedback is always better.

name: Measured-response closing
old: Observed-input removal and noise controls quantify how response predictability depends on available partners (Supplementary Fig.~S34). Separate imposed-alignment fields establish that the anatomical dictionaries can support learning when the target lies in their span (Supplementary Fig.~S5). Neither supplies a positive control for endogenous teaching in the visual-response recordings. The measured ancestry-similarity test and the modeled transfer diagnostic together delimit what the present data can establish about biological use of the proposed routes.
new: Input-removal and noise controls test dependence on recorded partners (Supplementary Fig.~S34); imposed-alignment fields establish learning capacity when targets lie in the anatomical span (Supplementary Fig.~S5). Neither tests endogenous teaching. The empirical ancestry-similarity test and modeled transfer diagnostic therefore bound distinct biological claims.
